title: When It Gets Too Hot, Even Monkey Moms Say 'I Can't Do This Anymore'
summary: You know how grumpy you get when you're super hot and hungry? Now imagine being a monkey mom in a forest where all the fruit trees are drying up. That's what happened in Costa Rica during a terrible drought in 2015. Scientists who have watched white-faced capuchin monkeys for over 30 years saw something shocking: mothers who are usually very devoted started walking away from their crying babies. 'The mothers just looking down like 'Too much trouble' and walking off, abandoning their infants,' said researcher Susan Perry. It was a sign that even tough monkeys have limits. A new study looked at 33 years of data on these monkeys to see how weird weather changes their lives. They found that during extreme dry or wet seasons, big monkey groups have a harder time finding enough food. Normally, a big group can bully smaller groups and take over the best fruit spots. But during climate extremes, that advantage disappears—maybe because there's just not enough good food anywhere. The monkeys also fight more within their own group when food is scarce. The study suggests that climate change, which makes crazy weather like El Niño more intense, could really mess up monkey societies. Another scientist, Filippo Aureli, saw that during that same drought, lots of baby capuchins died, and spider monkeys stopped having babies altogether. 'With climate change, these extremes are going to be more frequent and intense,' he said. 'And we don't know what's going to happen.' It's a reminder that climate change isn't just about melting ice—it's about real animals making heartbreaking choices right now.
why_it_matters: This story shows that climate change affects not just ice and polar bears, but also animals close to us like monkeys, and their family bonds can break under stress.

White-faced capuchin monkeys are known for being smart and using tools.
El Niño is a natural weather pattern that makes the Pacific Ocean warmer and can lead to droughts in some parts of the world.
Article_Structure: WHO: White-faced capuchin monkeys, researcher Susan Perry, and others.
WHAT: Mother monkeys abandoned their babies during a severe drought.
WHERE: In a dry forest in Costa Rica.
WHY: Extreme weather, worsened by climate change, made food so scarce that mothers reached their limits.

perspectives.description: These observations show us how extreme stress can push animals to make choices that go against their usual nature.
It's so sad to see mothers abandon their babies; it shows how climate change is hurting the most vulnerable.
The increasing frequency of droughts like this is a clear sign that we need to address climate change to protect wildlife.
